section.title: Jonah Flees and the Storm
section.sectionRationale: The book's opening movement: God's call to Nineveh, Jonah's flight in the opposite direction, and the storm that God hurls after him. It runs from the word of the LORD to the moment the pagan sailors, not the prophet, end up worshipping the true God.
section.thesis: A prophet runs from the God of the sea and the dry land, yet God pursues him through a storm, and the very sailors he endangers come to fear and worship the LORD.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: the call and the flight; the storm and the sleeping prophet; the casting overboard and the sailors' worship.

units.label: The call and the flight
units.note: down to Joppa, down into the ship

verses.text: Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah son of Amittai, saying,
“Get up! Go to the {{gadol|great}} city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before Me.”

Jonah, however, got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD. He went down to Joppa and found a ship bound for Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went aboard to sail for Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.

units.label: The storm and the sleeping prophet

verses.text: Then the LORD {{hurl|hurled}} a great wind upon the sea, and such a violent storm arose that the ship was in danger of breaking apart.

The sailors were afraid, and each cried out to his own god. And they {{hurl|threw}} the ship’s cargo into the sea to lighten the load. But Jonah had gone down to the lowest part of the vessel, where he lay down and fell into a deep sleep.
The captain approached him and said, “How can you sleep? Get up and call upon your God. Perhaps this God will consider us, so that we may not perish.”
“Come!” said the sailors to one another. “Let us cast lots to find out who is responsible for this {{raah|calamity}} that is upon us.” So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.
“Tell us now,” they demanded, “who is to blame for this calamity that is upon us? What is your occupation, and where have you come from? What is your country, and who are your people?”
“I am a Hebrew,” replied Jonah. “I {{yare|worship}} the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land.”
Then the men were even more afraid and said to him, “What have you done?” The men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them.

units.label: Cast into the sea, and the sailors' worship
units.note: the storm quiets, the pagans fear the LORD

verses.text: Now the sea was growing worse and worse, so they said to Jonah, “What must we do to you to calm this sea for us?”
“Pick me up,” he answered, “and {{hurl|cast}} me into the sea, so it may quiet down for you. For I know that I am to blame for this violent storm that has come upon you.”
Nevertheless, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea was raging against them more and more.
So they cried out to the LORD: “Please, O LORD, do not let us perish on account of this man’s life! Do not charge us with innocent blood! For You, O LORD, have done as You pleased.”
Then they picked up Jonah and cast him into the sea, and the raging sea grew calm.
Then the men {{yare|feared}} the LORD greatly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows to Him.

gadol.gloss: Great, large. The word runs like a drumbeat through Jonah: the great city, the great wind, the great storm, the great fish, the sailors who fear greatly. It keeps the reader's eye on the sheer scale of what God is doing.

hurl.gloss: To hurl or throw with force. The same verb describes the LORD hurling the wind, the sailors hurling the cargo, and Jonah being hurled into the sea. God and the storm are the true actors; everyone else is thrown about by the wind He sends.

raah.gloss: Evil, disaster, or calamity. The same word names Nineveh's wickedness in verse 2 and the calamity the sailors dread here. It threads through the whole book, binding together human evil, the disaster it deserves, and God's response.

yare.gloss: To fear, revere, or worship. Jonah claims to fear the LORD even as he flees Him, while the pagan sailors move from being merely afraid to fearing the LORD greatly with sacrifice and vows. The irony is sharp: the outsiders worship, the prophet runs.

basic.context: God tells His prophet Jonah to go and preach to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, Israel's most feared enemy. Instead Jonah runs the opposite way, boarding a ship for Tarshish. So God sends a great storm. The heart of the scene is surprising: the pagan sailors end up worshipping the true God while His own prophet sleeps and sulks.
basic.hermeneutics: This really happened, and the New Testament treats Jonah as a real person and his experience as a real sign. People debate whether the book is straight history or a pointed story, and whether a fish could swallow a man, but the point the writer presses is the same either way: you cannot flee the presence of God, and His mercy reaches even our enemies.
basic.originalLanguages: A few Hebrew words do a lot of work. God hurls the wind, the sailors hurl the cargo, and Jonah is hurled overboard, all the same word, tul, so God is clearly the one in control. The word great, gadol, keeps repeating: great city, great wind, great fish. And Jonah says he fears the LORD, yet it is the sailors who truly come to fear Him.
basic.typology: Jonah asleep in the storm, then thrown into the deep so that others may live, foreshadows Jesus asleep in a boat in a storm, and Jesus given up to death so that many are spared. Jesus Himself points back to Jonah as a sign.
basic.christ: Jesus calmed a storm with a word, showing He is the God of the sea that Jonah confessed. And where Jonah was thrown into the deep for his own sin, Jesus went willingly into death for the sins of others, the true and greater Jonah who saves those in the boat with Him.
basic.god: We learn that God is sovereign over the wind and the waves, that He pursues His runaway servants rather than abandoning them, and that His concern reaches far beyond Israel to pagan sailors and a wicked city. He is a God who will not let His people flee Him.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 139 says there is nowhere we can flee from God's presence. Mark 4 shows Jesus asleep in a storm and stilling it. Acts 10 shows the same God opening the door of mercy to the nations.
basic.oneStory: From the start Jonah shows that God's mercy was always meant to spill beyond Israel to the nations. A reluctant prophet, pagans coming to worship, a rescue through one man given up to the sea: it all points forward to the gospel going out to the whole world through Christ.

context.literary:
The book of Jonah is a short narrative built with unusual care, and chapter 1 is the first of its two matched halves. Chapters 1 and 2 tell the story at sea, chapters 3 and 4 the story at Nineveh, and each half opens with almost the same sentence: 'the word of the LORD came to Jonah', with the same command to 'get up' and 'go to Nineveh'. The first time Jonah goes the wrong way. The second time, 3:3, he goes. Reading chapter 1 well means hearing it as the first half of a diptych.

Within the chapter the movement is a descent. Jonah 'went down' to Joppa, verse 3, he had 'gone down' into the lowest part of the ship, verse 5, and in chapter 2 he will go down to the roots of the mountains. The verb of going down keeps pace with his spiritual decline, and the command to 'get up' is repeated in the mouths of God, 1:2, and of the captain, 1:6. Notice who is doing what. The pagan captain says almost exactly what God said to Jonah, and he says it to a man who is asleep.

The narrator also loves irony and contrast. A prophet of the LORD is passive and silent, while idolaters are pious and talkative. The sailors pray before Jonah does. Jonah speaks only twice in the chapter, to confess and to ask to be thrown overboard. The fear also grows in three steps: the sailors are afraid of the storm, verse 5, then of the God of Jonah, verse 10, then they fear the LORD in worship, verse 16. The chapter is shaped as a movement of the nations from terror to faith while the prophet moves the other way.
context.historical:
Jonah son of Amittai is a historical prophet. 2 Kings 14:25 identifies him as 'the prophet from Gath-hepher' who spoke a word that came true in the reign of Jeroboam II, when Israel's boundary was restored 'from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah'. That places him in the first half of the eighth century BC, in the northern kingdom, in a period of recovery and national pride. A prophet of good news for Israel's borders is now asked to carry a word to its enemy, which helps explain the reluctance.

Nineveh was a great city of Assyria, and its reputation was formidable. Genesis 10:11 says it was founded in the earliest days of the nations. Nahum, a century or so later, calls it 'the city of blood, full of lies, full of plunder', Nahum 3:1. Assyria was the empire that would destroy the northern kingdom in 722 BC and carry Israel off, 2 Kings 17. To an Israelite, being told to go and warn Nineveh was like being asked to help the enemy at the gate.

Tarshish lay at the far western edge of the known world. It is mentioned in connection with ships and with metals, Isaiah 23:1 and Ezekiel 27:12, and is often identified with a region in southern Spain, though the Bible does not say so. The point in the story is geography: Nineveh is east, so Jonah sails as far west as the world allows. Joppa was the port on the coast from which such a voyage began, and it is the same harbour in which Peter will later receive a vision about unclean food, Acts 10:9-16.

The sailors are a mixed crew calling on 'his own god', each one, which reflects the ordinary religion of the Mediterranean. They treat the storm as a religious problem, which is why they cast lots. That custom is well known in the Bible, Proverbs 16:33, and people of the day took it as a way of letting the divine speak.
context.canonical:
Jonah is a curious book to meet in the Prophets, because most of it is story rather than oracle, and the story has strong links in both directions. The theme of fleeing from God's presence is picked up in Psalm 139:7-10, which asks, 'Where can I flee from Your presence?' and answers that even at 'the farthest sea' God's hand will hold fast. In Jonah the psalm is lived out: the farthest sea is where he is found.

The storm and the sailors have a close relative in Psalm 107:23-30, where men go out in ships and see 'His wonders in the deep'. A tempest rises at God's word, the sailors' courage melts, 'then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble', and He calms the storm. Jonah 1 is a longer, odder version of the same hymn, with the twist that the one who should lead the worship needs rescuing too.

The call to Nineveh reflects a broader pattern. God told Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3, and Jonah's reluctance shows how slowly Israel absorbed the promise. Jonah's later words in 4:2 repeat the great self-description of Exodus 34:6, 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion', as the reason he ran. The principle that makes the warning to Nineveh sensible is stated in Jeremiah 18:7-8, where a nation warned of disaster that turns from evil finds God relents.

The New Testament makes Jonah a sign. Jesus refuses a sign to a wicked generation 'except the sign of the prophet Jonah', Matthew 12:39-41, and Luke 11:29-32 stresses that the men of Nineveh will condemn that generation because they repented, and 'now One greater than Jonah is here'. Mark 4:35-41 reads like a conscious reply, a storm, a sleeper, a frightened crew, and One who is greater.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author of Jonah wrote for an Israel that was comfortable with a God who loved them and uneasy about a God who also loved their enemies. Chapter 1 begins that argument without ever stating it. The author lets the reader sit with a man who knows the right theology and does the wrong thing. Jonah can say perfectly, 'I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land', verse 9, and in the same breath be a runaway. The author wants the hearer to feel how it is possible to confess a creed with the lips while fleeing its claims with the feet.

The author also means to unsettle assumptions about who is near to God. The sailors begin as strangers to the LORD and end by offering sacrifices and vows. The prophet starts as God's spokesman and ends as the cause of a calamity. The point is not that the sailors were better people but that God can make Himself known to anyone, and that His servants are not exempt from needing to be pursued.

A third intent is more gentle. Everything in the chapter is done by God: He speaks, He hurls the wind, He directs the lot. The author wants the hearer to trust that the God who pursued Jonah is the same God who will deal with Israel, and that being pursued is a mercy, because a God who let you flee would have given you up.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Jonah's flight is described, not recommended. The narrator never excuses it, and the rest of the book shows how it ends. The sailors' conduct is also described, not commanded: casting lots to find a culprit, and throwing a man into the sea, are what these men did in an emergency. Nobody should take the chapter as a warrant for deciding guilt by chance or for sacrificing a person to appease a storm.

What does carry forward is the pattern of how God deals with a disobedient servant and with unbelieving neighbours. The reader learns that running from an unwelcome calling is not safe, that God uses even the failure of His people to bring others to Him, and that a believer who sleeps through a crisis has no right to be indignant at those who pray. The captain's rebuke, 'How can you sleep? Get up and call upon your God', can fairly be heard as a word to the church, as long as it is applied with humility, since the rebuke came from a pagan to a prophet.

Jonah's confession and his readiness to be thrown overboard are exemplary in one narrow way, his honesty about his own guilt, and not in the motive that may lie beneath it.

debates.question: Is the book of Jonah history or a didactic story?

views.label: Straightforward history
views.case: Jonah is a named historical prophet, 2 Kings 14:25, and Jesus speaks of the men of Nineveh who repented and of Jonah's three days as real events, Matthew 12:39-41. The most natural reading takes the account as reporting what happened.

views.label: Didactic narrative or satire
views.case: The book's heavy irony, symmetry, and satirical portrait of the prophet lead some to read it as a theological story making its point through art rather than reportage.

debates.bearing: The message stands either way, but the New Testament's appeal to Jonah as a sign fits most naturally with reading the events as real; the writer plainly intends to teach, whichever genre is granted.

debates.question: Why did Jonah flee?

views.label: Fear for his own safety
views.case: Nineveh was a violent city, and a lone Israelite preaching against it might expect to be killed. This is the first explanation a reader reaches for, and verse 2 does say its wickedness has come up before God.

views.label: Reluctance for Nineveh to be spared
views.case: Jonah himself says in 4:2 that he fled because he knew God to be gracious and slow to anger and feared that He would relent. The chapter withholds this reason on purpose, and the reader is meant to learn it later. Jonah's prophetic work for Jeroboam II, 2 Kings 14:25, gives the nationalist colour to the view.

views.label: Both, in different degrees
views.case: A fear of the task and a dislike of its likely result need not exclude each other, and the narrator may deliberately leave the motive layered.

debates.bearing: Chapter 4 supplies the stated reason, so the second view has the best claim, but the first view is not an idle guess. What matters for chapter 1 is that nothing Jonah feared could justify leaving God's presence, and that his flight is a form of disobedience, not prudence.

debates.question: Is Jonah's request to be thrown into the sea noble or evasive?

views.label: Honest and sacrificial
views.case: He admits that he is the cause of the storm, verse 12, and offers his own life so that the sailors may live. This is the single most admirable moment in the chapter, and it echoes the substitution that the New Testament picks up.

views.label: A preference for death over obedience
views.case: Jonah never offers to turn the ship around and go to Nineveh. He chooses the sea over the mission, which fits his later wish to die in 4:3. His honesty is real but it falls short of repentance.

debates.bearing: Both readings can be held together: the offer saves the sailors and exposes the prophet. The tension is one of the chapter's quiet lessons, that a good act and a stubborn heart can sit in the same man.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word worth pausing on is the verb 'get up', qum. God uses it in verse 2, 'Get up! Go to the great city', and Jonah obeys it in the letter, 'Jonah, however, got up', verse 3, but toward Tarshish. The captain then uses it again in verse 6. Same word, three speakers. It becomes clear that the narrator wants us to see how an obedient-looking verb can carry a disobedient action. The same call comes again in 3:2, and the second time Jonah gets up and goes the right way.

The verb 'go down', yarad, is the spine of the chapter. He goes down to Joppa in verse 3, and the Hebrew says he has 'gone down' into the hold of the ship in verse 5. In chapter 2 he says 'I went down' to the roots of the mountains. The Bible uses this verb for descents into the grave, and the reader hears the rest of the story in advance.

Verse 4 contains a charming personification the BSB cannot keep. The Hebrew says the ship 'thought' it would break apart, as if the vessel itself were afraid. It is a small touch, but it fits a story where wind, sea, lot, fish, plant and worm all show more responsiveness to God than the prophet does.

The sleep of verse 5 uses a verb of deep sleep, radam, from the family of the word God uses when He puts Adam into a deep sleep in Genesis 2:21. The chapter's most dangerous hour finds the prophet in a heavy, unnatural slumber.

The captain says, 'Perhaps this God will consider us', and the little word 'perhaps', ulai, is a mark of the pagan's humility before a god he does not control. The king of Nineveh will say something similar in 3:9, 'Who knows?'. The unbelievers in the book reach for hope by guessing, while the prophet knows God's character exactly and resents it.

In verse 9 Jonah calls himself 'a Hebrew', ivri. The word is mostly used by outsiders, or by Israelites speaking to outsiders, for example in Genesis 39:14 and 1 Samuel 4:6, so it fits the occasion. His description of God as maker of 'the sea and the dry land' uses the word for dry land, yabbashah, from the creation account of Genesis 1:9-10. He says the LORD made the very thing that is now trying to kill them.

The sailors' prayer in verse 14 uses the phrase 'innocent blood', familiar from the law, Deuteronomy 21:8, and their line 'You, O LORD, have done as You pleased' echoes Psalm 115:3. The covenant name, the LORD, is now on foreign lips. And the twin acts of verse 16, sacrifice and vows, are the same two Jonah will promise in 2:9, so the sailors do before Jonah what Jonah only says he will do.

typology.fulfillment: Jonah sleeps in the hold while the storm threatens to sink the ship, Jonah 1:5. Jesus sleeps 'in the stern' on a cushion, Mark 4:38, and is woken with a question not unlike the captain's. The escalation is that Jonah's sleep is indifference and Jesus's is rest in His Father's hand, and where Jonah has to be thrown into the sea to quiet it, Jesus quiets it with a word, Mark 4:39. The type falls short because Jonah's sleep is a failing and Christ's is not.

typology.type: The man given to the sea so others may live
typology.fulfillment: Jonah's offer, 'Pick me up and cast me into the sea', and the sea's calming, verse 15, form a picture of substitution. Caiaphas unwittingly states the principle, 'it is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish', John 11:50. Christ is that one man, but where Jonah dies for his own guilt, Christ dies for the guilt of others. The type falls short because Jonah deserved the sea and Christ did not.

Jonah's repeated descents are an unwilling pattern of what Christ does willingly. Philippians 2:5-8 traces how He 'emptied Himself' and 'humbled Himself' even to death on a cross, and Ephesians 4:9-10 speaks of His descent 'to the lower parts of the earth'. The correspondence is the direction of travel, down. The contrast is the motive: Jonah descends in flight from a mission, Christ in obedience to one.

typology.type: Pagan sailors who fear the LORD and offer sacrifice
typology.fulfillment: The nations coming to worship the God of Israel. The scene is a small preview of Acts 10 and 11, where a Gentile household is given the Spirit, and of the vision of Revelation 7:9. It is a limited type, since the sailors have only just met the LORD and we are not told that their faith lasted, but it shows the direction God is moving.

study.christ:
Chapter 1 does not look to Christ by prediction. It looks to Him by pattern and by contrast, and Jesus Himself invites the reading when He calls Jonah the only sign He will give, Matthew 12:39. The chapter supplies four lines of connection.

The first is the storm. Mark 4:35-41 sets Jesus in a boat on a squall with the disciples, and the parallels are deliberate. A great windstorm, a sleeper below the deck, a frightened crew who wake him with a cry about perishing, 'Teacher, don't You care that we are perishing?', Mark 4:38, answering Jonah 1:6, 'Perhaps this God will consider us, so that we may not perish.' And the aftermath is the same: in Mark 4:41 the disciples are 'overwhelmed with fear', and the Greek wording matches the Septuagint's phrase for the sailors' fear in Jonah 1:16, 'they feared a great fear'. In Jonah the LORD sends the storm and the sailors fear Him. In Mark the one in the boat stills the storm and the disciples fear Him. The Gospel quietly says that Jesus does what only the LORD does. Psalm 107:29 had already given the line, 'He calmed the storm to a whisper', and now a Carpenter says 'Silence! Be still!'

The second line is substitution. Jonah tells the sailors to throw him in, 'so it may quiet down for you', verse 12. The sea becomes calm the moment he is gone, verse 15. Here is a picture of one life offered so that others might be spared. The qualification is as important as the picture: Jonah is thrown over because the storm was his fault. Jesus is not thrown over for His own sin but for ours, 1 Peter 3:18, and He goes willingly, John 10:18.

The third is the greatness of the greater Jonah. Jesus says 'One greater than Jonah is here', Matthew 12:41. Jonah was a reluctant prophet who preached to Nineveh and was disappointed when it repented. Jesus is the willing Prophet who weeps over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41, and who pursues enemies to the cross, Romans 5:10. Jonah went the other way from his mission; the Son 'came into the world' to save.

The fourth is the missionary pattern. The prophet who fled the Gentiles is succeeded by the Servant who is a light to the nations, Isaiah 49:6, and in Acts 10:9-16 Peter is made to go from the harbour of Joppa to a Gentile house, where the Spirit falls. A caution: we should not turn every detail into a code. The ship, the lot and the captain are part of the story's realism, and the links to Christ rest on what the Gospels themselves say.
study.god:
Chapter 1 gives a portrait of God that is unsentimental and warm at the same time.

He is a God who speaks first. 'The word of the LORD came to Jonah.' Nothing in Jonah's life prompts the call; it is pure initiative. The Hebrew idiom puts the word coming as an event, and Jonah's own refusal cannot stop it from arriving.

He is the God who sees. 'Its wickedness has come up before Me.' The language is like the outcry of Sodom in Genesis 18:20-21, where God says the cry 'has reached Me' and goes down to see. God is not indifferent to evil in a foreign capital. He is neither a tribal deity nor an absentee. The same awareness appears again in 4:11, where He knows how many people there are in Nineveh and also their cattle.

He is the God who is sovereign over the natural order without effort. 'The LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea.' Elsewhere He appoints a fish, a plant, a worm and an east wind. Winds, lots and seas obey, and the sailors' words in verse 14 are exactly right: 'You, O LORD, have done as You pleased.' The theology of Psalm 115:3 is dramatised. Proverbs 16:33 says the lot's every decision is from the LORD, and here it falls where He wills.

He is the God who pursues rather than abandons. His response to the runaway is not to find another prophet but to go after this one. The storm is an instrument of love as much as of discipline, since it turns Jonah's disobedience into the occasion for faith in others and, eventually, for Jonah's own rescue. Psalm 139:7-10 is not merely a truth about God's omnipresence but an account of His tenacity.

He is the God of the nations. The sailors are not told to convert; they are given a storm and a witness, and they respond. The question 'Is God the God of Jews only?', Romans 3:29, is quietly answered before it was asked.

Two tensions keep the picture honest. First, God uses a storm that endangers innocent sailors, and the sailors fear for their lives; the narrative allows that for His purposes, and ends with their safety and worship. Second, God's patience with Jonah stands beside His severity, and neither cancels the other. For worship the chapter asks us to stand with the sailors rather than with the sleeper: to fear the LORD with a great fear, to offer sacrifice, to make vows, and to trust that the God who made the sea and the dry land is the God who also holds us.

crossReferences.note: Jonah son of Amittai from Gath-hepher spoke a word that restored Israel's border under Jeroboam II. It confirms that Jonah was a historical prophet of the northern kingdom and a bearer of good news for Israel, which sharpens the surprise of being sent to Israel's enemy.

God says the outcry against Sodom has reached Him and He will go down to see. Jonah 1:2 uses a similar picture of wickedness 'coming up' before God. In both places divine knowledge of evil comes before judgment, and in both a servant of God is brought into the matter.

'Where can I flee from Your presence?' The psalm gives the doctrine, the chapter gives the case study. Jonah tries to go away from the LORD's presence by ship and finds that the farthest sea is still within the reach of God's hand.

Sailors on mighty waters see God's wonders in the deep, cry out in their trouble and are brought to the harbour. The pattern is exactly that of Jonah 1, where the sailors' cry in verse 14 is answered by the calm of verse 15, and where the shape of the storm becomes a school of faith.

'The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.' It supplies the theology behind the sailors' lot in verse 7. The pagan crew trusted chance, but the book shows that the lot fell by God's direction and landed on the right man.

If a nation God has warned turns from its evil, He relents of the disaster He planned. It states the principle on which Jonah's mission rests: a warning of judgment is an invitation, which is why Jonah fears it will work.

Jesus gives the sign of Jonah and says the men of Nineveh will rise to condemn an unrepentant generation, because 'One greater than Jonah is here.' It makes Jonah's story a witness in the final judgment and a pointer to Christ.

A windstorm, a sleeper in the boat, a cry that they are perishing, and then a great fear. The echoes of Jonah 1 are many, and the difference is that this time the sleeper stills the sea with a word, showing that Jesus occupies the place Jonah's God occupies.

Caiaphas says it is better that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish. He meant it as political expediency, but John treats it as unwitting prophecy. It is the logic of Jonah 1:12-15, one man for the many, and finds its true referent in Christ.

Peter, praying in Joppa, the harbour Jonah left from, is told not to call anything impure that God has made clean. The harbour where a prophet fled from the Gentiles becomes the place where an apostle is sent to them.

study.oneStory:
Jonah 1 belongs to the great problem the Bible keeps returning to: how a holy God deals with a world that has turned away, and how the people He has chosen are to serve that purpose. The promise at the root of Israel's calling was that the nations would be blessed through Abraham, Genesis 12:3. For a long while Israel kept the promise and forgot the mission. Jonah is the story of what that forgetting looks like in a prophet, and of how God does not abandon His purpose when His servant refuses it.

It answers the fall in a specific way. In Genesis 3 the man hid from the presence of the LORD God among the trees, and God came looking. In Jonah 1 the man runs from the presence of the LORD by sea, and God again comes looking, this time through the wind. The pattern is the same, a creature who flees and a Creator who pursues, and it will not end until the pursuer has the final word. The Babel story of Genesis 11 scattered the nations in pride, and the sailors, assembled from many peoples and each crying to his own god, are what the scattered world looks like. Yet it is these scattered people who first pray in the right name.

It prepares redemption. The sea that nearly swallowed the ship settles when the guilty man is given up to it. The New Testament places that pattern in Christ, who was given up, and says that the nations will find in Him what the sailors found in the calm: the God who made the sea and the dry land, and who saves. Jesus's own comparison, 'One greater than Jonah is here', makes the book a doorway to the cross and the empty tomb, and the great commission, Matthew 28:19, is the order Jonah refused, given to people who are told to obey it.

It looks to the new creation. In Revelation 7:9 a great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language stands before the throne, and the sea, for so long the symbol of chaos and threat, is gone from the new heavens and new earth, Revelation 21:1. The sailors with their sacrifice are a first, small foretaste of that crowd. The church lives in the time between: sent, like Jonah, to people we may not like, with a God who has already gone before us into the storm.

sermon.title: Man Overboard!
sermon.why: Part of Begg's expository series A Study in Jonah, this message works through the storm and Jonah being cast into the sea, Jonah 1:4-17, showing God's sovereign pursuit of His fleeing prophet and His mercy toward the pagan sailors. A clear, orthodox treatment of this movement.

quiz.q: Why did Jonah flee toward Tarshish?

options.text: He did not want Nineveh, Israel's enemy, to receive God's mercy.
options.note: Jonah 4:2 tells us plainly: he fled because he knew God was gracious and would relent.

options.text: He was simply afraid of the dangerous journey to Nineveh.
options.note: Fear may have played a part, but the book names his real reason as resentment of God's mercy.

options.text: He had not actually heard God's call clearly.
options.note: The call was unmistakable; Jonah deliberately went the opposite way.

options.text: God had given him no reason to go at all.
options.note: God gave a clear reason: Nineveh's wickedness had come up before Him.

quiz.q: What does the repeated Hebrew verb tul, to hurl, show about the storm?

options.text: God is the true actor: He hurls the wind, and everything else is thrown about by it.
options.note: The same verb for the wind, the cargo, and Jonah keeps God at the centre of the scene.

options.text: The storm was a violent but ordinary weather event.
options.note: It was violent, but the text presents it as sent by God, not merely natural.

options.text: The sailors caused the storm by their poor seamanship.
options.note: The sailors are competent and desperate; the storm is God's doing.

options.text: The storm had nothing to do with Jonah.
options.note: The lots and Jonah's own words tie the storm directly to his flight.

quiz.q: What is striking about how the pagan sailors respond?

options.text: They move from fearing the storm to fearing and worshipping the LORD with sacrifice and vows.
options.note: The outsiders end up worshipping the true God while the prophet runs from Him.

options.text: They calm down once the cargo is thrown overboard.
options.note: They do lighten the ship, but the point is their turning to the LORD, not their seamanship.

options.text: They abandon their gods only out of superstition.
options.note: The text presents genuine reverence for the LORD, not mere superstition.

options.text: They remain hardened and never acknowledge God.
options.note: They fear the LORD greatly and offer sacrifice, the opposite of hardness.

quiz.q: How does Jonah in the storm point forward to Jesus?

options.text: Jonah asleep in the storm and given to the sea foreshadows Jesus asleep in a storm and given up to death to save others.
options.note: Jesus Himself makes Jonah a sign of His death and resurrection, Matthew 12:39-41.

options.text: Both simply happened to be caught in bad weather at sea.
options.note: There is a real echo, but it is more than coincidence; it is a deliberate pattern.

options.text: Jonah is a perfect model of obedience for Jesus to follow.
options.note: Jonah is disobedient here; Jesus is the greater and obedient Jonah.

options.text: There is no connection between Jonah and Jesus.
options.note: Jesus explicitly links Himself to the sign of Jonah.

quiz.q: What does Jonah's confession in verse 9 reveal?

options.text: He knows the LORD made the sea and the dry land, yet he is trying to flee that very God across the sea.
options.note: His theology is right while his life contradicts it, the book's central irony.

options.text: He is a faithful worshipper with nothing amiss in his walk.
options.note: His words are true, but his flight shows his heart is far from obedient.

options.text: He does not really believe in the LORD at all.
options.note: He confesses the LORD genuinely; his problem is rebellion, not unbelief.

options.text: He worships many gods like the sailors.
options.note: He confesses the one LORD, the God of heaven, over against their many gods.

questions: Jonah ran because he did not want his enemies to receive mercy. Is there anyone whose repentance and blessing you would secretly rather not see? What does that reveal about your own heart?
Jonah's theology was right, he knew who God was, but his life was running the other way. Where is there a gap between what you say you believe about God and how you are actually living?
The sailors, outsiders to the covenant, ended up worshipping God while the prophet slept. Where might God be working in people you had written off, and how does that challenge you?
Jonah discovered there is no fleeing the presence of God. Where are you trying to go down and away from what God has clearly called you to do?
One man was given to the sea so the others could live, and that points to Jesus given up for us. How does resting in His rescue free you to stop running and obey?

translationNotes.note: Tarshish was likely a distant port in the western Mediterranean, the opposite direction from Nineveh; the point is that Jonah flees as far as he can from the task and from God's presence.
I worship translates the Hebrew for I fear, the same root used of the sailors; Jonah claims to fear the LORD in the very act of fleeing Him.
The men rowed hard renders a Hebrew phrase literally meaning the men dug in, picturing their desperate effort to reach shore rather than throw Jonah over.
